title: EXCLUSIVE: “Will the Madrid job give Mourinho his fire back? He feeds off the crowd,” says ‘Mourinho’ producer Miles Coleman
description: Miles Coleman, the producer behind the new Netflix documentary ‘Mourinho’, sat down for an exclusive interview with Managing Madrid’s Lucas Navarrete to discuss the “Special One’s” enduring legacy. Over the course of the conversation, Coleman pulls back the curtain on a two-and-a-half-year production process, revealing that Mourinho was granted no editorial control over the final […]
fullText:
Miles Coleman, the producer behind the new Netflix documentary 'Mourinho', sat down for an exclusive interview with Managing Madrid's Lucas Navarrete to discuss the "Special One's" enduring legacy. Over the course of the conversation, Coleman pulls back the curtain on a two-and-a-half-year production process, revealing that Mourinho was granted no editorial control over the final cut—a decision that led to moments of raw tension when the film challenges the manager's recent record. From the "burnout" of the record-breaking 100-point season to the psychological weight of the 2012 Champions League exit and the deliberate calculations behind his media persona, Coleman provides a rare, behind-the-scenes look at a man who is making his return to the biggest club in world football.

Please note that this article contains selected highlights from the discussion and does not include the interview in its entirety, which you can access through the Managing Madrid Podcast.

Navarrete: What have the general reactions been like on social media? I know the Madrid fan base has been very positive, but how are Chelsea or Inter Milan fans responding?

Coleman: The reaction has been very good. I was actually dreading the social media response because football is so tribal. In the series, we show both the positives and the negatives—the moments when things went well and when they didn't. I expected fans to be protective, but it has turned into a wonderful nostalgia trip. We've even seen Liverpool fans saying that while they "hated" the guy, the series was incredibly entertaining because it brought back so many memories. We woke up to find we were number one in the U.K., which is a great feeling.

Navarrete: Nostalgia is definitely a major factor here. We are talking about a man whose first stint at Chelsea was decades ago and who left Madrid 15 years ago. I have to admit, I'm generally not a fan of the "single-character" documentary format because it can often feel like a PR piece that avoids the negatives. However, I think you threaded the needle perfectly here by addressing the friction that comes with a character like Mourinho. How did you manage that balance while having him involved in the show?

Coleman: I appreciate that because it was one of the hardest parts of the project. The criticism of biographical documentaries is often that they are too "chummy" or hagiographic. From day one, we told Jose this couldn't just be a positive PR piece. While we had his cooperation and interviewed him for many hours, he never had editorial control. He didn't have the right to approve the final product; we told him, "It's not your film; it's for the audience. He is a smart man who understands how the media works, and he knew that if he had "sign-off" power, the product wouldn't be legitimate. This allowed us to push him on subjects he didn't necessarily want to discuss, such as Iker Casillas, Eva Carneiro, or even his father. We wanted to take the audience on the same journey we went on as fans—starting with the "Special One" aura at Chelsea and gradually increasing the pressure as his career progressed. I challenge anyone to watch the third episode where our director, Joe, essentially calls the second half of his career a failure. The tension in the room was so thick you could cut it with a knife. We wanted to be balanced. A lot of people who dislike Mourinho just wanted three hours of him being called a narcissist, but that would be unfair to a man who has been remarkably successful and changed the game.

I challenge anyone to watch the third episode where our director, Joe, essentially calls the second half of his career a failure. The tension in the room was so thick you could cut it with a knife. We wanted to be balanced.

Navarrete: Did you get the feeling that Mourinho connected most deeply with the Chelsea players?

Coleman: I actually think his strongest connection was with the Inter Milan squad. At Inter, he took a team that no one expected to win the Champions League and brought them to unbelievable glory before leaving at the very top. At Chelsea, there was "unfinished business" because they never won the Champions League together. You can hear it in John Terry's voice; he still feels a sense of guilt over the match that led to Jose's first sacking at Chelsea. At Inter, Jose also felt he had something to prove after being sacked by Chelsea and being passed over for the Barcelona job in favor of Pep Guardiola.

Navarrete: I think his reception at the Bernabéu will be very positive because nostalgia tends to filter out the negatives. However, did you address the "fiascos," such as the 2011 Champions League press conference, the Guardiola rivalry, or the incident with Tito Vilanova?

Coleman: We spoke to him about all of it. As a filmmaker, the challenge is deciding which details serve the macro story. We focused on the "symbolic" moments. Regarding Vilanova, he viewed it as a "rush of blood" and a bad moment where he felt provoked. It's always hard to leave things out, but we had to focus on the bigger narrative of his time in Madrid.

Navarrete: What about the 2012 penalty shootout against Bayern Munich? He has called that one of the worst nights of his career.

Coleman: We discussed it. He still seemed baffled that three of the most brilliant, psychologically strong players—Cristiano Ronaldo, Kaká, and Sergio Ramos—all missed. He didn't seem "haunted" by it, but rather viewed it as the ultimate example of the helplessness a manager feels during a shootout. Our focus for the Madrid years was largely on the domestic battle for supremacy with Barcelona and how he pushed that squad so hard they almost "burned out" to win the league with 100 points.

He didn't seem "haunted" by the penalties against Bayern, but rather viewed it as the ultimate example of the helplessness a manager feels during a shootout

Navarrete: He had a very contentious relationship with the Spanish press. Did you address that?

Coleman: Yes, we even interviewed Diego Torres, perhaps the journalist most critical of him. Jose felt that while he was loved in England, he was not loved by the media in Spain. The media scrutiny in Spain is on another level, and the exhaustion of his third season was largely due to those pressures.

Navarrete: It's been odd because he hasn't had a formal presentation or press conference yet. Do you think he has the energy to face the Spanish media again?

Coleman: With Jose, everything is deliberate. If he isn't speaking to the media, it's a calculation. He used the media brilliantly in England to help his team win. If he thinks being close to the media doesn't help his team win in Spain, he won't do it.

Navarrete: Where do you think this second tenure goes?

Coleman: The story of Mourinho is that everything that makes him brilliant also sows the seeds for his downfall—his intensity, his aggressiveness, his uncompromising desire to win. It's hard to imagine him still being there in ten years. The question is how quickly it turns. He often creates an "enemy" within the squad to motivate the group. The challenge now is that players have more power than they did 20 years ago. If a manager calls out a modern player, that player can just wait him out. It will be interesting to see Jose at a club that is truly bigger than he is again. And I think in in some ways I wonder if the Madrid job will give him some fire back where previously it was just harder to do that.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Listen to the full interview here on the Managing Madrid Podcast.

title: Jayden Daniels sends LSU a cease-and-desist after Pickett given No. 5
description: Former LSU football QB Jayden Daniels sent a cease-and-desist to LSU after LSU cornerback DJ Pickett was allowed to wear the No. 5.
fullText:
Former LSU football quarterback Jayden Daniels isn't happy with the Tigers' decision to let LSU cornerback DJ Pickett wear Daniels' No. 5. According to a report from ESPN, an attorney, on behalf of Daniels, sent a cease-and-desist letter to LSU saying the university can no longer use Daniels' name, image, and likeness. ESPN reports the letter was sent to LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry on Aug. 5.

Daniels spent two years at LSU, leading the Tigers to 10 wins in 2022 before posting historic numbers in 2023, en route to winning the Heisman Trophy.

The No. 5 went unused at LSU in 2024 and 2025, but as LSU began fall camp, Pickett was spotted in the jersey. LSU head coach Lane Kiffin said getting to wear No. 5 "was promised" to Pickett during Pickett's recruitment.

"I'm not going to judge something [that was done] when I wasn't here. But when a kid is promised something to come to a school, he should wear it. So at that point, I don't think that's really my decision. We should honor what he was told," Kiffin said at his weekly press conference.

Pickett signed with LSU in 2025 and wore No. 3 as a freshman. Pickett enjoyed a breakout season with the Tigers and is expected to be among the top defenders in the SEC this fall.

The letter, which ESPN obtained, said Daniels "made it clear that he did not want his number given to another player, and he believed his wishes would be respected."

Daniels was the third player in LSU history to win the Heisman Trophy, joining Billy Cannon and Joe Burrow. Cannon's No. 20 is retired and no longer worn. Burrow's No. 9 hasn't been issued since Burrow won the Heisman in 2019, but the No. 9 isn't officially retired.

The letter to LSU is essentially telling the program to stop using Daniels' likeness in any promotional materials.

title: Galatasaray reject massive €130m Al-Hilal bid for Victor Osimhen, insist star striker is not for sale this summer
description: Galatasaray have reportedly rejected a €130m bid from Al-Hilal for Victor Osimhen.The Saudi Pro League side submitted the massive verbal offer for Osimhen on Wednesday through intermediaries, but sa...
fullText:
Galatasaray have reportedly rejected a €130m bid from Al-Hilal for Victor Osimhen.

The Saudi Pro League side submitted the massive verbal offer for Osimhen on Wednesday through intermediaries, but saw the proposal rejected.

Galatasaray have informed Al-Hilal that the club have no intention of negotiating a potential sale this summer, reportSky Sports.

Osimhen has scored 59 goals in 74 games since signing for the Turkish Süper Lig champions from Napoli on an initial loan deal in 2024. That loan was made permanent for a Turkish transfer record fee of €75m last summer.

Al-Hilal have a long-standing interest in Osimhen and came close to signing the forward prior to his move to Istanbul.

The Saudi side want to bring in Osimhen to strengthen their squad ahead of a challenge for the Pro League title in 2026/27. Al-Hilal finished second last season, two points behind champions Al-Nassr.

The club are expected tosanction the exit of Darwin Nunez in the coming days, with Osimhen targeted as a high-profile signing to bolster the attack.

Al-Hilal have already completed a £60m deal to sign Crysencio Summerville from West Ham United and have Karim Benzema and Malcolm as part of their attacking options.

However, Galatasaray have emphatically insisted that Osimhen is not for sale at any price this summer.Tottenham Hotspur have been linked with a potential move for the Nigeria international.

title: Celtic handed Alistair Johnston injury blow ahead of crucial LASK play-off
description: Celtic have been dealt a potential injury blow ahead of their Champions League play-off against LASK, with Alistair Johnston reportedly a “major doubt” for next week’s first leg.9th August 2026;...
fullText:
9th August 2026; Rugby Park, Kilmarnock, Scotland: Scottish Premiership Football, Kilmarnock versus Celtic; Alistair Johnston of Celtic

The Canada international was withdrawn at half-time during Sunday's 5-1 Premiership victory over Kilmarnock after picking up a problem.

Assistant manager Shaun Maloney played down concerns immediately after the game, saying: "He felt a niggle and was taken off as a precaution."

However, the Scottish Sun now reports that Johnston could be facing a spell on the sidelines, placing his involvement against LASK in serious doubt.

It would be a significant setback for Martin O'Neill, particularly given Johnston's injury problems last season. The 27-year-old has started Celtic's opening two league matches this term despite continued transfer interest from Everton.

Celtic welcome LASK to Glasgow next Wednesday before travelling to Austria for the return leg six days later, with a place in the Champions League league phase at stake.

Should Johnston miss out, Anthony Ralston and Colby Donovan are O'Neill's main options at right-back.

title: How Mets new slugging prospect is striving to fix ‘last glaring hole’ in his game
description: New York Mets outfield prospect Aidan Smith was acquired from the Tampa Bay Rays in the Freddy Peralta trade.
fullText:
BROOKLYN, N.Y. — Mets outfield prospect Aidan Smith knows that he won't reach his full potential until he cuts down on his strikeouts.

This season, before Smith was traded from the Rays to the Mets in the Freddy Peralta deal, the 22-year-old was punching out in a career-high 32% of his plate appearances with Tampa Bay's High-A affiliate. In 49 games, he hit .215 with a .693 OPS.

In 2025, Smith had a 31.2% strikeout rate at the same level while batting .237 with a .719 OPS across 102 games.

JOIN OUR METS COMMUNITY: IT'S FREE ON YOUTUBE!

"I feel like that's the last glaring hole [in my game] and something I can get better at," Smith told NJ.com before his home debut with High-A Brooklyn on Tuesday.

What gives Smith a "really high ceiling," as Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns put it last week, is the rest of his tools. Smith, who is now ranked as the Mets' No. 12 prospect by Baseball America, is an above-average runner and defender. There may be holes in his swing, but he has legitimate pull-side pop.

This is the same prospect who was considered the headliner in the Randy Arozarena trade from the Mariners to the Rays ahead of the 2024 deadline. That year, at just 19, Smith slashed .288/.401/.473 with 11 home runs and a 143 wRC+ over 97 games in Class-A with Seattle and Tampa Bay.

"My first year was a great year and I ended it on a high note with the Rays," Smith said. "Last year, I went a little down, but I learned a lot from it, and really, I think got better on the mental side of the game. It's helping me with my success now."

Smith has made quite a first impression in his first week in a Cyclones uniform. He swatted four home runs in his first six games with Brooklyn while stealing two bases and spending time at all three outfield positions.

Still, the strikeouts have persisted. Smith has struck out 10 times in 30 at-bats over his first seven games in the Mets' system.

This top Mets prospect grew up a die-hard fan. Here's why he could be their shortstop of the future.Aug. 13, 2026, 7:00 a.m.

Francisco Lindor has message for Mets on his future, direction of franchiseAug. 12, 2026, 2:28 p.m.

"You're never going to be able to be perfect," Smith said, "but if I can at least limit some of that and give myself opportunities to get hustle singles in the infield or draw walks, whatever it may be, I think that's going to really elevate me."

Smith explained that he's working on making better swing decisions. In the cage, coaches pepper him with different types of pitches. Out on the field in batting practice, he approaches each pitch as though he's ahead in a 2-0 count. Those situations force him to be stubborn and wait for the pitch he's looking for in his wheelhouse. When he does get those pitches over the plate, the goal is to put a good swing on them and drive them.

"Swinging at the right pitches and swinging at the right pitches that you're good at hitting," Smith said. "More often than not, you're gonna hit balls you want to hit and those lead to homers."

title: This top Mets prospect grew up a die-hard fan. Here’s why he could be their shortstop of the future.
description: New York Mets shortstop prospect Sammy Stafura was acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates in the Luke Weaver trade.
fullText:
BROOKLYN, N.Y. — When Sammy Stafura first found out that he had been traded from the Pirates to the Mets in exchange for reliever Luke Weaver, the top shortstop prospect was in the middle of a seven-hour bus ride.

Stafura and his High-A Greensboro teammates were en route to Rome, Ga., scheduled to play the Braves' affiliate the next day.

What followed was a travel nightmare. Stafura sat restlessly for the final four hours of that bus trip only to hop off and take an Uber for an hour and a half to the Atlanta airport. He then flew back to Greensboro and packed up all his stuff before getting back on the road to meet High-A Brooklyn for their road series in Wilmington.

JOIN OUR METS COMMUNITY: IT'S FREE ON YOUTUBE!

It was only then, once he got settled with his new team, that he was able to truly process the news.

Stafura grew up a Mets fan in Westchester County. He still considers himself a "die-hard" to this day, the type of fan that watches the big-league club as much as he possibly can.

Even after he was drafted in 2023 by the Reds in the second round out of Walter Panas High School in Cortlandt Manor, N.Y. and subsequently dealt to the Pirates in the Ke'Bryan Hayes deal last summer, that love for the Mets never went away.

"My room was painted bright orange for the Mets," Stafura told NJ.com ahead of his home debut with the Cyclones on Tuesday. "My mom keeps sending me photos. I was always wearing Mets stuff, always watching the Mets."

Stafura's favorite Mets memory was New York's World Series run in 2015, watching those games with his entire neighborhood. Another was in 2024 when Stafura was watching the Mets' thrilling comeback win over the Brewers in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series from Slovakia, where both of his parents are from. Granted, he didn't get to see Pete Alonso's game-winning home run live.

"The second before Devin Williams was picking his leg up [to pitch], my Wi-Fi just turned off, so I didn't know what happened for like an hour!" Stafura said with a grin. "I was trying to scramble finding Wi-Fi and then I saw the Mets won. It was crazy!"

All that makes the onboarding process much easier for the Mets as they welcome several new prospects into the organization after their trade deadline selling spree. They won't need to spend any time teaching Stafura about the franchise he's now representing.

"I'm going out there and I'll run through a wall for this team," Stafura said. "I'm gonna give them everything I got. This is for the city. This for the town. This for everyone. This for the Mets. So, that's what I'm gonna do. I'm gonna bring the energy and I'm gonna give 100% whatever I got that day."

As much of a dream come true as this opportunity is for Stafura and his family, this 21-year-old shortstop has the potential to make this much more than a feel-good story.

Stafura, who is now ranked as the No. 9 prospect in New York's farm system by Baseball America, was having a breakout summer before he was acquired by the Mets. Over 47 games with High-A Greensboro, the shortstop hit .301 with a 1.021 OPS, 19 home runs and 16 stolen bases. He homered 14 times in the month of July alone.

I asked Sammy Stafura, who grew up a diehard Mets fan, to build his all-time favorite Mets lineup. 

A few of his picks might surprise you…

Watch my full interview with Stafura on Speaking of the Mets right here: https://t.co/cBi3bnq5V2 pic.twitter.com/kXLQ206qix

Don't forget the rest of his tools. As one National League scout put it this week, Stafura's floor is higher than most because of his speed and defense at a premium position.

Stafura flashed both of those above average skills in his home debut at Maimonides Park on Tuesday night. He flew down the line to beat out an infield single in his first at-bat. A few innings later, he knocked a ball down in the hole to his right and fired a strike across the diamond for the out.

"I think the first thing that jumps off the page with Stafura is the defense," Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns said on deadline day. "He's got tremendous defensive ability. He's a very good base runner. Can impact the game in a variety of different ways, help you win ballgames in a variety of different ways and clearly he has power as well.

"When you begin to talk about a power hitting infielder who we believe can play shortstop at a high level, that's a player with a pretty high ceiling."

While he's been on fire at the plate for the last few months, Stafura isn't a finished product offensively. The right-handed hitter is striking out nearly 30% of the time with chase and swing-and-miss tendencies that can put him in bad counts. That same scout called those trends "worrisome" and said that he'll need a "better approach."

So, how was Stafura able to explode for such a power surge recently then?

"Stafura is an ambush hitter," the NL scout said. "He went a month where he got into good counts and hit the mistakes."

Clearly the Mets are confident in Stafura's upside. Not only did they part with Weaver, who has another year of team control and would've been a valuable piece of their bullpen next season if they didn't move him, but they reportedly ate $8 million of the reliever's remaining salary.

Asked what's been working so well for him at the plate of late, Stafura singled out his mindset. He's digging into the box looking to do damage — trying to hit the ball hard, far and into the gap — and the results have followed.

How Mets new slugging prospect is striving to fix 'last glaring hole' in his gameAug. 13, 2026, 8:24 a.m.

Francisco Lindor has message for Mets on his future, direction of franchiseAug. 12, 2026, 2:28 p.m.

"I went up there thinking I'm the best, knowing that I'm the best and that's just the attitude I brought to the field every single day past few months," he said. "I think that's what's helped me a lot in the past few months. And I'm going to keep doing that every single day, going out there, trying to be aggressive, trying to battle. I'm going to play offense up there, not going to play defense."

If this continues, don't be surprised if Stafura gets a taste of Double-A action before the end of this season. Cyclones manager Eduardo Núñez certainly won't be shocked if Stafura gets that call soon.

"He's got 20 bombs and he's hitting almost .300," Núñez said with a smile. "He has already demonstrated that he can handle whatever is here in the South Atlantic League. Hopefully he does well for a couple days and maybe he gets a call to move up. I don't think he needs to prove anything here."

title: DTM calendar 2027 announced: No internationalization for now, clashes with WEC
description: The DTM has presented the calendar for the 2027 season: how Formula 1's exit from Zandvoort will have an impact and which clashes there are with other series
fullText:
The DTM has officially presented its calendar for the 2027 season - and it does so without a ninth race weekend on international soil, with which series organizer ADAC had actually wanted to expand the calendar. Instead, the series remains loyal to its eight venues and, as in 2026, will start from April 23 to 25 in Austria at the Red Bull Ring, with the traditional season finale in October at Hockenheim.

The weekend in Oschersleben, which had hosted the season opener in recent years and this year marked the start of the second half of the season, returns to the beginning of the season. The race weekend will take place from May 7 to 9, just two weeks after the opener in Spielberg.

This now makes Oschersleben the second stop on the calendar, while the DTM's second foreign guest appearance in Zandvoort in the Netherlands will from now on mark the start of the second half of the season, meaning the two races swap places on the calendar.

This is made possible by the fact that Formula 1 will no longer race in Zandvoort. Extensive preparation work was needed for the Grand Prix in the Netherlands, which meant the DTM had only limited date options available on the North Sea circuit in summer.

In 2027, the series' Netherlands guest appearance will take place from August 6 to 8 - around two weeks before this year's Formula 1 date in Zandvoort.

The Lausitzring, which is to be renovated, will continue to host the third weekend of the season from May 18 to 20, while the season highlight at the Norisring will traditionally take place on the first weekend in July (July 2 to 4).

After Zandvoort as the start of the second half of the season, the calendar order remains the same as in 2026: At the Nurburgring, the decisive phase of the championship will be ushered in from August 20 to 22, at the Sachsenring a preliminary decision can already be expected from September 24 to 26 - and at the Hockenheimring, the finale will traditionally take place from October 8 to 10.

The fact that, despite ADAC's efforts, there is no additional weekend abroad this year can be attributed to the fact that, despite a large number of interested parties such as Brno in the Czech Republic or venues in Italy, it is not at all easy to find a racetrack that can guarantee spectators and is also of interest to DTM stakeholders.

In addition, the teams pushed back because of the high costs of an additional race weekend. ADAC has therefore decided to continue relying on the events of the existing calendar, all of which have so far been able to show rising spectator numbers compared with 2025.

"The excitement in the grandstands show that the DTM is on the road to success and is hugely appealing to spectators. We have seen a 13% growth in the number of visitors in the first five events of this year. We want to carry that momentum into the 2027 season and are sticking with tried-and-tested venues that are popular with visitors. However, we are varying the order", explains ADAC motorsport directorThomas Voss.

"With eight top-class race weekends, racetracks steeped in tradition, and a balanced mix of national highlights and international outings, we are once again able to offer fans, teams and partners a calendar that is right out of the top drawer."

What about clashes with other racing series and endurance classics? The DTM and the GT World Challenge Europe avoid each other as usual. However, the DTM weekend in Oschersleben overlaps with the 8h race in Austin, which also takes place from May 7 to 9 and counts toward the Intercontinental GT Challenge (IGTC) in 2027.

There are also clashes with the World Endurance Championship: The second WEC weekend at Silverstone, which takes place from April 23 to 25, clashes with the DTM season opener in Spielberg. The same applies to the WEC guest appearance at Fuji and the DTM's Sachsenring weekend from September 24 to 26. This makes a GT3 program for drivers in both series difficult to implement.

The DTM, however, avoids the three endurance classics at Le Mans, the Nürburgring and Spa - and there is no clash with the Le Mans test on June 6 either.

However, a Formula E program will be difficult for DTM drivers to implement in 2027: There are two clashes with the electric racing series' calendar (May 8 to 9: Oschersleben vs. Berlin; June 18 to 20: Lausitzring vs. Zandvoort).

In the US IMSA series, the clash between the DTM season finale and the endurance classic Petit Le Mans on October 9 is particularly significant. In addition, there is an overlap between the DTM weekend at the Nürburgring and the IMSA race in Virginia on August 22. However, this only affects the GTD Pro and GTD drivers who contest the entire series.

title: ‘It’s time to change’ – Fabrizio Romano teases major shift to football transfer reporting after window closes
description: Fabrizio Romano has revolutionised football transfer reporting, building an enormous global following around his ability to break major moves. Romano first broke the news of Mauro Icardi’s move to Inter Milan in 2011 and has since become the world’s most recognisable football reporter.
fullText:
Fabrizio Romano has revolutionised football transfer reporting, building an enormous global following around his ability to break major moves.

Romano first broke the news of Mauro Icardi's move to Inter Milan in 2011 and has since become the world's most recognisable football reporter.

The Italian journalist has amassed more than 100 million social media followers and popularised the now-famous catchphrase, "here we go".

Romano has continued to break several huge stories throughout the summer, but his latest comments suggest a major change to his approach is on the horizon.

Fabrizio Romano celebrated the success of his report on Ronald Araujo's loan move from Barcelona to Liverpool on LinkedIn.

His exclusive story racked up 49 million views, two million likes, 47,000 comments, and was shared two million times.

However, in the same post, Romano hinted that this could be his final summer as a football transfer reporter.

He wrote: "I'm probably not gonna continue into the transfer market industry as I'm doing right now for longer: it's time to change the approach, the view…

"But this will be another topic soon, after the transfer window closes. But still, these numbers feel incredible.

"The adrenaline of the breaking story, the exclusivity, the unexpected factor, from zero links at all to done deal… well, this will always remain unmatched for me. Onto the next one!"

Whatever comes next for Romano, the football landscape would certainly look different without one of its loudest voices.

fullText:
Chelsea need to ask themselves if their intention is to sell Malo Gusto or not as potential suitor are put off by the price.

If you enjoy Talk Chelsea coverage and want to see more of it, add us as a preferred source on Google to make us a favourite and see more of our content.

Our writer Simon Phillips has an interesting piece out today on his Substack about Malo Gusto.

The full back has been linked with moves away from Chelsea this summer, but nothing concrete has come up. Manchester City were linked most strongly, but the massive asking price put on the Frenchman is putting off any bids for him.

Malo Gusto (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images)

The most crucial piece of information in there is the list of clubs who have expressed interest in Gusto. Manchester City had been established already. But also named are Bayern Munich, Liverpool, Tottenham, PSG and Juventus.

It doesn't matter how many teams are interested, however, if the price remains at £75m. Nobody is going to pay that, or anything close to that. Gusto's value is only going to fall if he spends a year on the bench behind Palestra and Reece James.

Landon Emenalo is a player gaining more and more attention in the game because of his exceptional talent. He's lining up a first senior loan move.

Trevoh Chalobah has left Chelsea, and his comments earlier today were the first time we've heard him speak since leaving the club where he spent 20 years.

title: 'Saints gamble Mubama needs to step up'
description: Could Manchester City striker Divin Mubama's loan spell at Southampton be just what he needs to make the step up to being a true first-team player?
fullText:
Could Manchester City striker Divin Mubama's loan spell at Southampton be just what he needs to make the step up to being a true first-team player?

The 21-year-old was ever-present in Stoke City's matchday squad last season, but a serious leg injury in January meant he made only one further Championship appearance for the club.

He will be hoping to play a bigger role during his time at St Mary's and BBC Radio Solent's Adam Blackmore feels it could be reminiscent of recently departed Saints midfielder Shea Charles' time at Sheffield Wednesday.

Charles, who also came up through City's academy, played 44 games for the Owls during his breakthrough season on loan from the Saints.

"This season for Mubama needs to be that season for Shea Charles," Blackmore said.

"It needs to be the time that he grows up, steps up, handles men's football. If he gets it right, he's got bags of talent, so I think it's a good gamble from Saints."

title: 'Ravindra Jadeja will punch me, but he is on the wrong side of thirty': Ex-India cricketer's blunt take
description: Murali Kartik believes Manav Suthar possesses the skills to succeed Ravindra Jadeja. Suthar has shown promise with both bat and ball in recent matches. Jadeja is nearing the end of his distinguished Test cricket career. India is looking for future spin bowling options as Jadeja's time winds down. Suthar's emergence offers a promising prospect for the team's long-term strategy.
fullText:
Former India spinner Murali Kartik believes Manav Suthar has the qualities required to eventually take over from Ravindra Jadeja in India's Test side.

Jadeja and Suthar are both part of India's squad for the upcoming Test series against Sri Lanka, with the two left-arm spinners expected to feature in the playing XI for the opening Test in Galle later this week.

With Jadeja now 37, Kartik feels India must already be looking at the next phase of their spin-bowling attack. He identified Suthar as a potential long-term option, particularly because of the youngster's ability to contribute with both bat and ball.

Suthar made his Test debut earlier this year and made an immediate impact, finishing with seven wickets, including a six-wicket haul against Afghanistan in Mullanpur.

He also impressed in India's recent three-day warm-up game against SLC XI, taking two wickets and contributing 45 runs. His first-innings score of 41 further underlined his all-round ability.

Kartik, however, was keen to assess Suthar on his own merits rather than draw direct comparisons with Jadeja.

"I think he is a very, very good bowler. Let's not compare him with anybody. He is old-school; he has many things going very well for him. For me, I was jumping with joy when I was doing that game against Afghanistan, because I was calling that game, and for me to see somebody release the ball like that and have that kind of consistency and have that kind of skill," Kartik told reporters in an interaction organised by Sony Sports Network.

"After a very long time, we are seeing a bowler like that. Maybe for India, it has come at a good time," he added.

Kartik also highlighted the timing of Suthar's emergence, given Jadeja's career is approaching its final phase.

"Ravindra Jadeja will punch me the next time he meets me, but at the end of the day, he is on the wrong side of thirty. He is in the twilight of his career, and we don't know how much longer he will play. From that point of view, you are always looking at passing the baton," Kartik added.

Jadeja has already retired from Test cricket? no, he has already retired from Tests and is also out of India's ODI plans, according to the provided details. Since the Champions Trophy 2025, he has played only six matches in the format and picked up just one wicket.

With Suthar now in the Test setup and already having shown that he can contribute in both departments, Kartik believes India could have a promising option ready as the baton eventually changes hands.

title: 31 days till Arizona Cardinals' opener: Remembering the 1931 season
description: With 31 days until the Arizona Cardinals' 2026 opener, let's look back at their 1931 season.
fullText:
We continue the countdown to the start of the Arizona Cardinals' regular season. Today, Thursday, August 13, is 31 days away from the Arizona Cardinals' regular-season opener on Sept. 13 on the road against the Los Angeles Chargers.

With 31 days until Week 1, let's look back at the 1931 season for the Cardinals.

In 1931, the Cardinals started the season losing three games in a row. They rebounded by winning the next four games in a row and finished the season 5-4.

They had the league's No. 1 offense in yards and scored the second-most points in the league, averaging 13.3 per game.

They had the league's No. 1 defense in yards, but they were dead last in points allowed (14.2 ppg).

Fullback Ernie Nevers was one of three Cardinals All-Pros. He made the first team. Rookie center Frank McNally was also on the first team, while left guard Walk Kiesling made the second team.

Nevers scored eight rushing touchdowns, made 15 extra points and made the team's only field goal of the year. He also threw six touchdown passes.

description: Swansea City suffer a heavy blow on the eve of the new Championship season as scans reveal centre-back Cameron Burgess has suffered a ruptured Achilles.
fullText:
Swansea City have suffered a heavy blow on the eve of the new Championship season after scans revealed centre-back Cameron Burgess has suffered a ruptured Achilles.

Swansea say Burgess faces surgery and a "significant spell on the sidelines" after he limped off during their EFL Cup defeat to Birmingham City last weekend.

It may be that the 30-year-old misses the entire 2026-27 Championship campaign, though that depends on how well he recovers.

Burgess played every minute of league football last season after joining Swansea in the summer of 2025.

The Australia international, who featured at this summer's World Cup, was a mainstay of Swansea's defence alongside captain Ben Cabango.

In his absence, summer signing Stephen Welsh and academy product Filip Lissah are contenders to start at centre-back when Swansea begin the new league campaign at Stoke City on Saturday.

But the expectation is that the Swans will aim to recruit at least one more central defender before the transfer window closes.

title: Swiatek into first final of her 'toughest season'
description: Iga Swiatek will meet Elena Rybakina in the Canadian Open final after both players battled through their semi-finals in three sets.
fullText:
Iga Swiatek will meet Elena Rybakina in the Canadian Open final after both players battled through their semi-finals in three sets.

Six-time Grand Slam champion Swiatek withstood an Elina Svitolina comeback attempt to seal a 6-3 1-6 6-3 win in Toronto and reach her first WTA final of the season.

The Pole, 25, has not reached a final since winning Cincinnati 12 months ago and had only reached one semi-final this year.

"It hasn't been an easy season, probably the toughest one in my life," said seventh seed Swiatek.

"This week has been really positive and inspirational for me, and it always kind of shows that you need to keep going no matter what."

Later, Australian Open champion Rybakina sealed her place in the final, despite losing the opening set to Coco Gauff.

After winning four games in a row to clinch the second set, the world number two secured a 5-7 6-2 6-2 victory, having also come from behind to win her quarter-final against Naomi Osaka.

"I feel like in the first set we were playing well but then I rushed it a little bit," said 27-year-old Rybakina.

"I'm just glad that I managed to win again in three sets."

Friday's final will be the 13th professional meeting between Swiatek and Kazakh Rybakina, with both players winning six matches each to date.

In their last meeting - their only match of 2026 - Rybakina won in straight sets in the quarter-finals of her Australian Open-winning campaign.

On playing Swiatek, Rybakina said: "It's going to again be a very difficult match, and we know each other so well. We play so many times.

"In my case, I feel it's more again about the recovery after so many hours on the court, and bring as much energy as I can."

In the Canadian Open men's singles in Montreal, Ben Shelton will face fellow American Brandon Nakashima in the final after both players won their semi-finals in straight sets, against Learner Tien and Rafael Jodar respectively.

Victory for Nakashima would secure his first Masters 1,000 title and the most prestigious win of his career.

Shelton is looking to retain the title and win his seventh ATP tournament.

title: I do not have much time left in UFC - Makhachev
description: Islam Makhachev says he "does not have much time" left in the UFC as the Russian prepares to make the first defence of his welterweight title against Ian Machado Garry at UFC 330 on Saturday.
fullText:
Islam Makhachev says he "does not have much time" left in the UFC as the Russian prepares to make the first defence of his welterweight title.

The 34-year-old, who is widely regarded as one of the best MMA fighters of all time, faces Ireland's Ian Machado Garry at UFC 330 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on Saturday.

The former lightweight champion made his UFC debut in 2015 and has gone on to build a glittering resume, winning 17 of his 18 fights in the promotion.

Should he beat 28-year-old Machado Garry at the Xfinity Mobile Arena, he will eclipse Anderson Silva's 16 successive wins in the UFC - a record which has stood for 13 years.

Makhachev moved up in weight last year after a record-breaking fourth lightweight title defence and says he wants to compete more often as he enters the latter stages of his career.

"I'm not like young guy. Now it's better for me to fight every three to four months," Makhachev told UFC Hall of Famer Demetrious Johnson.

"I understand I'm not 28 years old; I'm 34 right now. And I don't have much time.

"Sometimes it's not going like you want in the UFC. You want to fight after three or four months, but it's not according to your wish."

Critics have debated in the build-up to Makhachev's bout with Machado Garry if his achievements have surpassed team-mate and coach Khabib Nurmagomedov.

Former lightweight champion Nurmagomedov retired in 2020 having won all 29 of his fights, with a relentless pressuring style which overwhelmed his opponents.

Makhachev is not as aggressive in the octagon as Nurmagomedov but is a more well-rounded striker, while his only defeat came against Adriano Martins in 2015.

In beating Jack Della Maddalena last year to become a two-division champion, however, Makhachev ticked off a goal which Nurmagomedov never achieved.

Earlier this week, UFC president Dana White said Makhachev is "on the right path" to being regarded as the greatest fighter in UFC history.

Machado Garry comes into the fight having won 10 of his 11 fights in the UFC and will become the first Irish champion in the promotion since Conor McGregor, should he defeat Makhachev.

A win would also see him surpass McGregor as the Irishman in the promotion with the most wins in history.

Makhachev has been mostly dismissive of Machado Garry's ability during fight week, but the Irishman says he's preparing for the biggest test of his career.

"I have so much love and respect for Islam Makachev and his body of work that he has done in the UFC. There is no other fight I would want to prove that I'm the best in the world," said Machado Garry.

"I get to fight the greatest lightweight of all time, a two-weight world champion, the number one pound-for-pound fighter on the planet.

"That's why the fight is so interesting. You have got one who focuses mainly on wrestling and grappling, the other who focuses on striking and anti-grappling. This is a fight for history. This is a fight for legacy."

title: Messi plays for Inter Miami after father's death
description: Lionel Messi makes a substitute appearance for Inter Miami on Wednesday following the death of his father and hinting he may retire.
fullText:
Lionel Messi made a substitute appearance for Inter Miami on Wednesday following the death of his father and hinting he may retire.

Messi's father Jorge passed away in his hometown of Rosario, Argentina last week at the age of 68 after a long illness.

In an emotional social media post, the 39-year-old Argentina forward said he was considering his future in football, adding he was "really not sure if I'll carry on doing it for much longer".

After attending the private funeral in Argentina on Sunday, Messi flew back to the United States and came on at half-time to huge cheers in Miami's 3-2 defeat by Leon in the final group game of the Leagues Cup.

Messi's most iconic moments as he ponders retirement

Messi unsure he will play 'much longer' after father's death

Messi was absent for Miami's 2-1 loss to Monterrey in the Leagues Cup on Saturday but made himself available to coach Guillermo Hoyos for the must-win game against Mexican side Leon.

It is the first time Miami have been knocked out in the opening phase of the competition since the Leagues Cup was expanded in 2023 - the year Messi arrived and they lifted the trophy.

Jorge was Messi's agent since he was 14, watching him become one of the sport's greatest ever players and at his side when he captained his country to World Cup glory in 2022.

Argentina reached the final of this summer's tournament but were beaten 1-0 by Spain in extra time. Messi wrote that his father urged him "to play in one last World Cup" despite his health deteriorating.

Miami midfielder Yannick Bright, who scored his side's second goal against Leon, called Messi's return "incredible", adding he and other team-mates just wanted to support their captain.

"I wasn't expecting it," Bright said. "It shows how much he cares. When I saw he was here, all I was thinking about was to give my 150% for him.

"It's a tough situation. We try to stay close to him and support him as much as we can, but it's a lot."

Leon coach Javier Gandolfi said Messi "is human being that is different to the rest".

He added: "Today he demonstrated once more what he's made of."

title: Golfer admits 'stupidity' after faking hole-in-one
description: An amateur golfer says he has "completely made a fool" of himself after admitting he faked making a hole-in-one at a tournament in the United States.
fullText:
An amateur golfer says he has "completely made a fool" of himself after admitting he faked making a hole-in-one at a tournament in the United States.

Zach Holland was due to play in a two-person team competition at WingHaven Country Club in Missouri when he fraudulently placed the ball in the cup at the fourth hole earlier in the morning, before his round.

Holland, who is a plus-two handicap, had completed the first three holes when he told his group he was going to have to take a phone call as his grandmother was ill, so he would run ahead to the next tee and hit his shot first to keep up with the pace of play.

When the rest of the group arrived at the par-three fourth, Holland said he had taken his shot, but claimed not to know where the ball had ended up.

When they found it in the cup, the group celebrated what they thought was a hole-in-one.

Speaking to radio station 101 ESPN, external in St Louis, Holland, who has now resigned his membership, said: "You do something as dumb as I did, there are consequences for that."

The member-member tournament - where both players must be official members of the same golf club or organisation - includes a hole-in-one prize pot.

When asked what the motivation was, Holland replied: "I don't really know. I've talked to people and there really is no motivation, just complete stupidity.

"We were giving two shots back to the field - and that's not an excuse, there is no excuse for what happened. But to answer your question, we were giving two shots back to the field, and I went about it just completely and utterly the wrong way."

Nathan Charnes, the acting PGA of America president and general manager at WingHaven, said in a statement to Golf.com, external the club had "promptly addressed the matter", adding they "care deeply about the integrity of the game and the experience we provide for our members and guests".

Holland's achievement drew scepticism in the clubhouse, as there were no witnesses who saw him do it. He finally admitted to what he had done when confronted by staff, who had security footage of him driving a car near the fourth hole before his tee time.

He did confirm, however, there was no footage of him actually placing the ball in the cup.

Holland, who is a former college golfer, continued: "I made a terrible mistake, the lack of moral character. I can take the banter and the chatter because I deserve that from a golf perspective.

"But what I am most worried about is my family, breaking trust with a marriage I have had for five years next month.

"We have two kids that are under three and you know, it's not fair to them for me to put them in that situation where they walk in a room, there is a stigma there that your dad [is a cheater]."

Holland was also asked had he ever done anything like this before. "No, not to this extent," he said.

When pushed to explain what he meant, he replied: "I'm not a cheater on the golf course. I made a bad decision and I have to suffer the consequences", before adding he was trying to move forward and protect his family.

title: Football Association of Ireland withdraws Infantino support
description: The Football Association of Ireland [FAI] officially withdraws support for under-fire Fifa president Gianni Infantino, while the Irish Football Association [IFA] confirms it backs Uefa's stance.
fullText:
The Football Association of Ireland [FAI] has officially withdrawn support for under-fire Fifa president Gianni Infantino, while the Irish Football Association has confirmed it is backing Uefa's stance.

On Monday, European football's governing body Uefa signed an open letter along with Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, accusing Infantino of breaking trust "through deception".

It follows an attempt by Infantino to sell a stake in Fifa's commercial operations to a private investment company - since abandoned - which has left his bid for a fourth term at top of world football in a perilous state.

Last week, the Welsh FA became the first home nation to withdraw support with the FA following days later.

The FAI - governing body for football in the Republic of Ireland - has confirmed it has also withdrawn support for Infantino in a letter to Fifa, having previously indicated its support prior to the post-World Cup controversy.

"Following an FAI board meeting, the decision was taken to rescind the letter of support that the Association supplied earlier this year," it confirmed.

"It has since written to Fifa to explain its reasoning.

"The Association is grateful for the support that Fifa provides to Irish football, but recent events have raised significant concerns regarding governance, transparency and the lack of meaningful consultation.

"Considering the governance challenges that the FAI has had to overcome in recent years, the Association feels a particular obligation to advocate for and uphold best practice."

Northern Ireland's body [the IFA] noted the "wider concerns" of those in football regarding Infantino and while it has not gone so far as to formally withdraw support, it is backing Uefa's stance.

"We take our responsibilities as a member association of both Uefa and Fifa seriously," said an IFA spokesperson.

"We support the current Uefa position on the matter and will continue to engage constructively on issues relating to football governance.

"We are of course aware of the recent developments and wider concerns within the football community. We are considering these matters carefully and will continue to engage through the appropriate governance structures and channels.

"At this stage, we have no further comment."

title: Critical former referees add to culture of fear, says retiring Taylor
description: Retiring Premier League referee Anthony Taylor says his decision to quit was partly due to the toxic debate around officials.
fullText:
Just five weeks ago, Anthony Taylor was centre stage at the World Cup - refereeing the last-16 match between Spain and Portugal in Dallas.

But now, for the first time in 20 years, he is not involved as an English football season gets under way.

From the outside, the turnaround from officiating at the highest level to retirement seems sudden.

Here, for the first time, the 47-year-old explains his decision in detail - opening up on the impact of the often toxic debate surrounding officiating, and the intense scrutiny faced by referees.

Taylor also says he thinks his fellow officials should think twice before criticising their former colleagues in the media and talks of his hopes of helping Turkish football emerge from a sprawling referee betting scandal.

And he reveals what he really thinks of the video assistant referee (VAR) system.

Football Daily - Taylor on retirement, career and scrutiny on referees

Taylor retired last month, announcing in a short statement the end of a career during which he officiated 668 matches in the English professional game, every major domestic cup final, and 163 international fixtures.

He wrote it had been "an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant".

"It was part of it," Taylor says when we meet at his lawyer's offices in Leeds.

"Any referee will be lying to you if they said that pressure or that scrutiny did not bother them, because that's a natural human reaction.

"One of the challenges that referees face at every level is actually understanding the challenges that we face.

"Fear of making mistakes, external opinion, spectators, managers, parents, media, colleagues. All these things feed into creating self-doubt, lacking confidence, and then things can spiral out of control and you lose the ability to actually have any confidence in what you're doing on the field."

For years, Taylor said he had developed "resilience" to handle the pressures he faced, but can that only last so long?

"Everybody will experience times where dealing with that environment for a long period of time, your energy levels would dip," he says.

"That then starts to impact on motivation and your actual confidence. It goes back to the confidence again of, 'I've got to go again, make sure I don't make a mistake, still want to get to this tournament or have this match'. It's a very real feeling that everybody would go through.

"I was very confident in my own coping mechanisms on how I dealt with that.

"The decision to retire is purely based on my body and my mind coming to its natural course in that current role - and it's ready to go on a new journey."

Having taken charge of three matches in his second World Cup, Taylor says he only decided to retire once his tournament ended, which seemed like "the perfect time".

He says he has not missed gruelling pre-season training drills, but admits to "a hint of sadness" because "that's a big part of my life that I'm going to miss being involved in".

"I wanted to decide when I finished on my own terms," he says. "And I don't think you can say there's any better place to finish than at the World Cup."

So are his family relieved? Last year, Taylor told BBC Sport they no longer went to his matches because of the abuse he received, and spoke about how they were targeted by Roma fans in Budapest Airport after the 2023 Europa League final.

"Undoubtedly one of the things that you are considering are the serious sacrifices that both your family and your friends have made over the years for you to do what you do," he says.

"Family life takes a back seat… so, for sure, that was a big part of why I decided to step back.

"It was in combination with... the scrutiny and the demands placed on referees at the very top level. And that doesn't necessarily mean that you're struggling to cope with those demands, but it comes to a point where it feels that your body and your mind needs to take a break from those kind of pressures."

Taylor has stayed off social media in recent years, but admits there is a limit to avoiding the scrutiny.

"Even away from social media, the general coverage of football these days is 24/7," he says. "So there's a lot more mediums for you to discover what people think about what happened last weekend.

"It's not always negative feedback when you come across fans and people when you're travelling around the country. But it is like you are living in a goldfish bowl for 10 months of the year."

Taylor says the scrutiny on officials is "off the scale", and much of that is from "people in the media looking for things to scrutinise, whether that be fairly or unfairly". He describes it as a "big snowball effect".

Does it disappoint him that includes former match officials?

"Yes, it does personally, because it doesn't have any balance to it a lot of the time," he says.

"It's just part of the focus that comes with football. When we're dealing with supposedly objective analysis of matches, whether that be an expert ex-player in a studio or an ex-referee, that should be balanced and fair.

"If it's all one-sided criticism, that creates a culture of fear, disrespect, shame.

"There's a thirst for people to be told: 'Is the decision right or wrong?' And the reality in football is there's a lot of subjectivity and opinion in the middle of right and wrong. But that's not acceptable a lot of the time now."

Asked if that means he will not go into the media, he adds: "I would never feel like I would be wanting to be in a place where I want to criticise somebody, because I'd like to think I've got a very good understanding of why somebody's made a decision that they've made.

"Of course, a wrong decision can be made. Nobody really chooses to understand the reasoning why.

"I feel my skills and my passion are better suited to trying to pass on that knowledge and experience I've been lucky enough to accumulate over the years."

Asked about allegations of favouritism during the World Cup involving other teams and referees, Taylor said: "It always saddens me when someone's integrity is questioned and they receive threats.

"[The] result of a football match is multifaceted. Of course, referee decisions are part of that, but we have players who have a low passing accuracy. We have players who miss penalties. We have coaches who maybe make the wrong tactical changes or the wrong team selection.

"So there's a huge range of factors that play into a result of the game. So I think it's probably important that people just need to remember that."

Taylor will be trying to pass on his knowledge and experience in Turkey, where he has been appointed director of elite refereeing for the country's football federation.

He will take up that role in the wake of a major refereeing scandal in the country, with a five-year investigation finding 371 of 571 match officials had betting accounts.

Asked how he can help the federation move on, Taylor says: "The main focus, working together with the president and chairman, is on helping the officials - particularly the younger officials in the group - develop, build that resilience, build a better skillset to cope with those demanding matches, and really to drive improvement of standards in that respect and that's the central aim of my role there.

"The role, in a nutshell, is about improving standards for the top-level group of officials in Turkey, along with helping them develop their talent ID programme and also helping their international referees improve, get better, more high-profile appointments. Which is something that excites me.

"I'm very privileged that people hold my experience and knowledge in such high regard that they think I can make such a positive impact.

While Taylor says his biggest regret is never having the chance to take charge of a Champions League final, he relished officiating at his second World Cup, though he found officiating in the extreme heat of Dallas "brutal".

Once again, VAR proved controversial at the tournament, with four new areas covered by the system.

"Anything to do with VAR is good when we're talking about increasing the overall accuracy of decision-making," says Taylor.

"But we also need to remember that VAR is there to create a sense of justice, so [for] the big clear errors, and it's not there for microscopic, long-detail checks. And that's probably where everybody's trying to work even harder to get to, particularly this coming season.

"I think if we continue to focus on not being microscopic and not being too long in checking situations, where we're only using really clear evidence of an error being made, then... yeah, I think people will start to accept and trust the process more."

Asked if it was being used too often, Taylor says: "I think most people agree that does happen on occasions, so it's very sensible for us to say that and acknowledge that sometimes things are taking too long, and we're being too microscopic.

"We don't need to take too long looking at stuff, and we need to act on really clear visual evidence to intervene and change the decision."

title: Fulham leave pitch as Malaga take penalty into empty net
description: Fulham's pre-season friendly against Malaga ends in chaotic fashion as the Premier League side leave the pitch before a penalty shootout.
fullText:
Fulham's pre-season friendly against Malaga ended in bizarre fashion on Wednesday, with the Spaniards taking a penalty into an empty net as Alvaro Arbeloa's side headed down the tunnel.

Malaga equalised in the last minute of normal time, when defender Calvin Bassey was penalised for a handball that allowed Eneko Jauregi to convert from the penalty spot to make it 2-2.

But that was only the start of the chaos.

Former Real Madrid boss Arbeloa was sent off for seemingly remonstrating with the referee at full-time but he headed straight down the tunnel with the rest of his players, who believed that the match was over.

But La Liga side Malaga were expecting a penalty shootout to follow, and remained on the pitch ready to decide the winner of the Costa del Sol Trophy.

With fans awaiting a shootout, striker Jauregi placed the ball on the spot and converted into an empty net before celebrating with his team-mates in front of the home support at Malaga's Estadio La Rosaleda ground in southern Spain.

Fulham maintain both sides agreed the match would end without a shootout should it end in a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

In a post-match report on Malaga's website, the La Liga club wrote: "Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract."

Fulham conclude their pre-season preparations against Stuttgart on Saturday.

title: ‘Nightmare fodder’: Roku’s AI slop channel is even worse than expected
description:
Fairground TV is a 24/7 channel devoted to low-quality AI content for viewers sick of watching real people move in ways that won’t haunt you
The appeal of Roku is that, whatever you happen to want to watch, there will almost certainly be a live channel for it. Just want to watch Little House on the Prairie? There’s a channel for it. Just want to watch Duck Dynasty? There’s a channel for that too.
fullText:
Fairground TV is a 24/7 channel devoted to low-quality AI content for viewers sick of watching real people move in ways that won’t haunt you

The appeal of Roku is that, whatever you happen to want to watch, there will almost certainly be a live channel for it. Just want to watch Little House on the Prairie? There’s a channel for it. Just want to watch Duck Dynasty? There’s a channel for that too. Purely want to watch nothing but local news from Wisconsin? Guess what: there’s a channel for that too.

But despite this wealth, a section of the population was still to see its needs fulfilled. What about people who hate plot and vision and the sight of people speaking convincing dialogue that synchronises perfectly with the movement of their lips? What about the people who just want to watch an unyielding torrent of eerily weightless nightmare fodder? Well, good news. Roku has finally caught up.

It was reported last week that Roku launched the Fairground AI Creator TV channel, the first free, all-AI streaming channel that pulls content from roughly 100 AI creators around the world. Early reactions were, to put it mildly, not great. The Verge compared it to eating from a trough, while Futurism called it “bottom-of-the-barrel slop”.

In truth, you will not watch Fairground AI Creator TV, and that’s sort of the point. This is television with vanishingly low production costs. Compare an hour of this cheap slop with, say, the tens of millions of dollars it takes to produce an episode of Stranger Things, and you’ll soon understand why executives might find the prospect irresistible. In this landscape you don’t need breakout hits, just enough stoned and curious students at 3am to turn a profit.

That said, I have actually just spent a few hours watching Fairground AI Creator TV, more out of self-hatred than anything else, and it would appear that the early reviews are right. On the plus side, the channel is evidence that artificial intelligence has come on in leaps and bounds over the last couple of years. Had this been attempted in 2023, we would have had a 24/7 feed of mutant Will Smith choking down handfuls of writhing spaghetti, and everyone would have vomited themselves dry. Generally speaking, what Fairground has to offer is much better.

However, it is still awful. Categorically, catastrophically awful. The channel doesn’t so much offer shows as a drifting dreamscape of bad ideas rendered as horribly as possible with no thought paid to scheduling. At one point on Wednesday, a shrill high-frequency anime gave way to a long and staid German-language short about Nazi bureaucracy. After that came a sort of Gladiator ripoff that had all the dynamism of an exhibit you’d see at the fourth-best museum on a poorly planned family holiday.

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

In fact, as an aside, there seems to be an awful lot of this. Switch on Fairground at any time of day and I’d estimate you are no more than 15 minutes away from seeing a witless, sepia historical drama of some description, full of craggy, burly men glowering at each other, dramatically lit by sunset regardless of which direction they’re facing. There is so much of it that it worries me about the future of the medium. The promise of AI is that it allows limitless story potential, and yet the bulk of it ends up looking like what would happen if your dad lucked himself a job scheduling Sunday afternoons on ITV3.

There are still horrible glitches to navigate – stray mouths that don’t move in time with dialogue, impossible physics, one specific instance of a man trudging through snow while his feet bizarrely made a clip-cloppy hoof noise – but these are becoming less and less frequent as the technology improves. The bad news about this is that you’re forced to concentrate on the storytelling ability of the people who made this. And you simply cannot.

Because it – all of it, every last stinking second of every godawful film – is completely inert. It is devoid of weight, of life, of vision and wit. The channel just flatly sits there, impressed by itself despite being physically unable to hold anybody’s attention. You may as well be watching a screensaver, a CD-Rom menu screen or a fridge.

The hope is obviously that something like Fairground will be the future of entertainment, churning out muck for pennies while an entire stratum of creatives go hungry. And who knows, one day it might achieve this. The technology is moving so quickly that it isn’t impossible to see it eventually developing the capacity to convincingly entertain.

But on the basis of what I’ve seen, that day is still a long way off. At one point, the channel cut away to a commercial for Roku’s Dr Phil channel, and the sight of an actual flesh-and-blood human acting in an identifiably human way almost moved me to tears. And surely anything that makes you emotional about Dr Phil of all people doesn’t deserve to exist.

title: We Can’t Surrender to Climate Destruction
description: Sarah...
fullText:
Politicians and pundits are telling us to accept the escalating breakdown of our planet. We have to fight back.

In July, Chicago’s air was so thick with smoke you could smell it and taste it and feel it in your throat. Health officials were telling us to stay inside as much as possible. People wandered around big-box stores looking for air purifiers. Parents shared tips on how best to protect their kids. The haze made the edges of buildings look less sharp and made your thoughts less sharp, too, as headaches and lightheadedness set in. There were also reports of increased hospital visits by people with conditions like asthma.

The situation in Chicago was caused by smoke from Canadian wildfires, which, science has made clear, are bigger and more catastrophic than ever because of human-made climate change. The fires spread destruction through Canada, with First Nations people bearing the worst, and along with wildfires in northern Minnesota, sent hazardous smoke into the United States from Minneapolis to New York. If summer is the season of splash pads and beaches and watermelon slices, it is also, increasingly, a time of mustard-tinted air, hiding in your home if you have one, and refreshing your air-quality-tracking app.

As the frequency of these apocalyptic scenes increases, regular people are scrambling—to get through their workday, to protect their loved ones, to figure out how to breathe cleaner air. Yet there is an astonishing lack of urgency among those actually in a position to do something about the climate crisis.

The message from our political and media class is unmistakable: Climate destruction, while perhaps not desirable, is the new normal, an inevitability. This message is obviously unacceptable, but the explanation for its growing prevalence cannot be reduced to platitudes about mass complacency or human adaptability. It is imposed by an elite that is institutionally unwilling to grapple with the stakes of what is happening.

A large majority of people on this planet are concerned about climate change. A 2024 study in Nature Climate Change found that, globally, 89 percent of people want their governments to do more to fight the climate crisis. And according to a 2026 study in Health Affairs Scholar, 65 percent of adults in the United States are concerned that climate change will harm their personal health.

These findings are borne out by anecdotal evidence. On July 17, Fabian Martin, a Chicago delivery worker, told me he had spent the previous day outside during the worst of the smoke. “The smoke is so dirty,” he said. “Imagine my lungs.” A friend texted me on the same day: “This is so apocalyptic. Makes me afraid for the future.”

Yet just as public concern is climbing, media coverage of climate change is plummeting. John Kotcher, the director of the Center for Climate Change Communication at George Mason University, said in February that “we have reached the lowest point in how often people hear about” climate change since 2015. The media critic Adam Johnson (full disclosure: He’s also my husband) found that there was no mention of the role of climate change in nearly two dozen nightly-news segments about the smoke and other extreme weather events on ABC, CBS, and NBC from July 13 to 19.

On the political level, the Republican Party remains outright denialist, while Democrats as a whole are talking about climate change less. A slew of Democratic Party–aligned think tanks, meanwhile, is encouraging politicians to adopt an even lighter touch. The billionaire-backed Searchlight Institute, for instance, recommended precisely that in a 2025 memo, “The First Rule About Solving Climate Change: Don’t Say Climate Change.”

It doesn’t have to be this way. The catastrophe of climate change is not inevitable. It is a human creation, and the people most responsible for driving it have names. They sit in corporate boardrooms and congressional offices. They remain sluggish and cavalier as their constituents choke on toxic air. Yet the scientific consensus is that the crisis can be mitigated if we stop extracting fossil fuels from the ground.

Achieving such a monumental change will certainly be difficult. It will require an economy-wide mobilization, a reconfiguring of how our society is organized, and, no doubt, a confrontation with capitalism. But nothing can compare to the hardship of what is to come if such action is not taken: Entire countries will be uninhabitable, and millions of people will die, with poor countries that did the least to cause the crisis hit hardest first (though, as we are seeing, people in “rich” countries will suffer greatly too).

More and more people are coming to understand this existential threat on a visceral level. It has entered our lives, and our lungs. The dread of heat and smoke and storms is becoming a normal part of summer. But normalcy should not be mistaken for acceptance. Our grim new routine, rather, is a screaming alarm that if we don’t stop the scourge of fossil-fuel extraction now, we will look back one day and remember this summer, when dangerous smoke enveloped millions, as the good times.
